what: Southern Copper mines copper in Peru and Mexico, and smelts and refines it itself. Molybdenum, zinc and silver come out of the same ore and are sold as by-products. It is controlled by Grupo México.
customers: Industrial buyers of refined copper and metal traders worldwide; copper demand comes from construction, electrical grids and vehicles.
money: mining, smelting and refining at operations in Peru and Mexico
molybdenum, zinc and silver recovered from the same ore
moat: Very large, long-life ore bodies with among the lowest production costs in the industry, and its own smelting and refining capacity.
risks: Profit moves directly with the copper price, which the company does not control
Community protests and permitting have delayed Peruvian projects for years
Mexican and Peruvian tax and royalty rules can change
Grupo México controls the company, so minority holders have limited influence
opportunities: Copper demand is rising with electrical grids, data centres and electric vehicles while new mines are scarce
Low production costs mean it stays profitable at copper prices that hurt competitors
Expansion projects in Peru and Mexico could lift output if permits are granted
watch: The copper price and whether the Tía María and other Peruvian projects move ahead.
